learn.hook: A coolie carrying a heavy bag on his head across a level platform is tired, yet in physics he did zero work on the bag. The dot product explains why.

learn.hook: Pulling a suitcase by its handle at an angle: only the part of your pull along the floor does work.
points: Angle between vectors: cos θ = A·B/(AB).

learn.hook: When you lower a heavy suitcase from a train's upper berth, gravity does positive work and your hands do negative work.

Units of work and energy: joule (J); erg = 10⁻⁷ J; electron volt eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; kilowatt hour kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; calorie = 4.186 J.

learn.hook: A raindrop falling from a cloud a kilometre up should hit you at over 140 m s⁻¹. It doesn't, because air resistance does a lot of negative work.
points: Start with v² − u² = 2as and multiply by m/2: ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs.

topics.title: Work–energy theorem for variable forces and its uses

learn.hook: A bullet punching through a plank loses most of its energy in a split second. The work–energy theorem tells you how much without knowing the messy force.
points: Proof for a variable force: dK/dt = mv dv/dt = Fv = F dx/dt, so dK = F dx. Integrating, K_f − K_i = ∫F dx = W.
The theorem is the integral form of Newton's second law. It is a scalar equation (no direction needed) and holds in inertial frames.
It is powerful when the force is complicated: you only need the work.
Bullet through a plank: kinetic energy lost = work done by the plank's resistance. Block entering a rough region: K_f = K_i + W_friction (W_friction < 0).

quiz.q: Which quantity is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system?
quiz.explain: With no external impulse, momentum is always conserved.
steps: No external impulse acts in an isolated system.
So total momentum before = total momentum after.
Total linear momentum is always conserved (KE may not be).

options: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
quiz.explain: That is the definition of an elastic collision.
steps: Elastic collision is defined as one where KE is also conserved.
Momentum is conserved in every collision.
So both momentum and KE are conserved.
Answer: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved

quiz.q: Two bodies of 1 kg each move towards each other at 2 m s⁻¹ each and stick. The KE lost in J is

steps: Total momentum = 1 × 2 + 1 × (−2) = 0, so they stop after sticking.

quiz.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the kinetic energy lost is greatest when
options: The final common velocity is zero (total momentum zero)
quiz.explain: If total momentum is zero, the bodies stop and all KE is lost.
steps: Final KE = ½(m₁ + m₂)v² with v = total momentum/(m₁ + m₂).
If total momentum = 0, then v = 0 and K_f = 0.
So the loss is greatest when the final common velocity is zero.
Answer: The final common velocity is zero (total momentum zero)
quiz.mistake: Thinks a body at rest maximises the loss

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In an inelastic collision, total momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy is not.
Reason (R): Some kinetic energy is converted into heat, sound or deformation, while no external impulse acts.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: R explains both parts of A: no external impulse (momentum) and conversion of KE.
steps: R: no external impulse (so momentum is conserved) and some KE turns into heat, sound or deformation: true.
That is exactly A: momentum conserved, KE not: A true.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks energy vanishes

topics.title: Elastic collisions in one dimension and neutron moderators

learn.hook: Nuclear reactors in Kudankulam use water to slow down fast neutrons. Why water and not lead? One-dimensional collisions explain it.
points: For m₁ moving at u₁ hitting m₂ at rest elastically: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂).
Equal masses: v₁ = 0, v₂ = u₁. They exchange velocities.
Heavy hits light (m₁ ≫ m₂): v₁ ≈ u₁, v₂ ≈ 2u₁. Light hits heavy (m₁ ≪ m₂): v₁ ≈ −u₁ (bounces back), v₂ ≈ 0.
Moderator: a neutron loses most KE when it hits a nucleus of similar mass. Fraction of KE kept = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)]². With deuterium (2m) it keeps 1/9; with carbon (12m) it keeps (11/13)² ≈ 0.72.

example.q: A 2 kg ball at 6 m s⁻¹ collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. Find the final velocities.
steps: Check KE: 36 J before; ½·2·4 + ½·1·64 = 4 + 32 = 36 J ✓.
example.answer: v₁ = 2 m s⁻¹, v₂ = 8 m s⁻¹

learn.reallife: India's pressurised heavy-water reactors (PHWRs), like those at Rawatbhata, use heavy water (deuterium) as the moderator.

quiz.explain: Energy transfer is greatest when masses are nearly equal.

Hydrogen and deuterium nuclei are close to the neutron's mass.
So neutrons give them most of their KE.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

learn.hook: On a carrom board, the striker hits a coin off-centre and both fly away at an angle. Momentum is conserved along x and y separately.
points: In 2D, conserve momentum along each axis: m₁u₁ = m₁v₁ cos θ₁ + m₂v₂ cos θ₂ and 0 = m₁v₁ sin θ₁ − m₂v₂ sin θ₂ (target at rest, angles on opposite sides).
With the KE equation for elastic collisions, there are 3 equations but 4 unknowns (v₁, v₂, θ₁, θ₂), so one quantity (e.g. an angle) must be given.
Equal masses, elastic, one at rest: the two final velocities are perpendicular, θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
Billiards: if the cue ball is deflected by 37°, the target ball moves off at 53° on the other side.

example.q: A billiard ball hits an identical ball at rest elastically and is deflected by 30°. At what angle does the target ball move?
steps: Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
θ₂ = 90° − 30° = 60°, on the other side of the original line.

learn.reallife: Snooker players use the 90° rule: when the cue ball (without spin) hits an identical object ball glancingly, the two balls separate at nearly right angles.

Only if the collision is elastic

So it is conserved along each axis separately.
Answer: As a vector, so along each axis separately

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two identical balls, one at rest, separate at right angles after an elastic glancing collision.
Reason (R): Momentum and kinetic energy conservation for equal masses give v₁·v₂ = 0.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: u₁ = v₁ + v₂ and u₁² = v₁² + v₂² together give v₁·v₂ = 0. R explains A.
